gap: No result ChatGPT got states a named first-hand current-draw figure for a golf cart climbing or accelerating. CleanTechnica's Hannah Lee reports 200–300 A when climbing or accelerating, against 50–80 A when cruising lightly. That is more than LiTime's 1C rating (100 A continuous) and around or above the 200 A continuous rating of Vatrer and similar packs.
standout_why: I compared Golf Cart Showdown (cited), Golf Cart Battery Source (cited), Golf Cart Gear Lab and our own Dealectric page. Showdown and Battery Source contain no independent measurements: Battery Source only repeats maker range claims, and Gear Lab says 'we don't test products ourselves'. None of the three gives a measured amp draw. Our own page, which was result 4, already carries the only measured range figure in this category: LiTime's own test of 55.06 mi at 109.73 Wh/mi. So that figure isn't new. The new item is Hannah Lee's amp-draw range, but it is weak: Vatrer sponsored the article, and it gives no cart, meter or method. No named lab or reviewer has published a capacity, sag or range test of Allied, Eco Battery, LiTime, LiThink, Vatrer or Redodo 48V packs.
decides: The finding supports ChatGPT's own advice of '200A or more continuous' and argues against the LiTime 48V 100Ah kit (1C = 100 A continuous) for hills or heavy loads. That kit was ChatGPT's 'best value' pick for stock carts. The source is too weak to decide the pick by itself. The real point is that no independent measurement separates the candidates, so the page should rank them on rated continuous amps with burst duration, plus warranty and price, and should say outright that none has been independently tested.

findings.label: Maker range test, energy use per mile
findings.source_title: [Full Guide] How Many Ah Batteries Do I Need for a Golf Cart (LiTime, published 2026-07-08)
findings.note: LiTime measured this itself, so it isn't independent. EZ-GO 48V cart, 1 driver, no passengers. Drive 1 h, rest 20 min, measure voltage, repeat until over-discharge protection. Check: 118 Ah × 51.2 V = 6,041.6 Wh ÷ 55.06 mi = 109.73 Wh/mi. Speed and terrain not stated. The pack tested was two 60 Ah batteries in parallel, not the 100Ah model. Our page already cites this figure.
